**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty smooth oriented link $L$, a compact oriented spanning surface $F$ with boundary $L$, and a smooth loop $J$ in $X=S^3\setminus L$ transverse to the interior of $F$.

[A1] Full AC is the ambient choice hypothesis for the Alexander-duality convention. [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] The link complement $X$ is connected, and Alexander duality identifies $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ with $\mathbb Z^r$ on the positive meridian basis; total linking is the sum of the component coordinates. [[lem-the-complement-of-an-oriented-link-is-a-connected-smooth-three-manifold]], [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

[F2] Smooth loops and homotopies in $X$ can be perturbed to be transverse to the interior of $F$, while a prescribed closed region on which the map is already suitable is kept fixed. [[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], [[prop-relative-transversality-preserves-a-map-on-a-closed-good-region]]

[F3] The degree-one Hurewicz map sends $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ onto $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$ and factors through abelianization. [[prop-the-first-hurewicz-map-in-degree-one-is-abelianization]]



**Given:** Full AC, $L$, $F$, $X$, $J$, and the conventions of the Statement.

1.1 Choose a basepoint $x_0\in X\setminus F$, which exists on a local side of any interior point of $F$. Represent any class of $\pi_1(X,x_0)$ by a smooth loop transverse to $\operatorname{Int}F$, using [F2]. Define $I_F$ on that class to be its signed intersection count. If two such loops are homotopic in $X$, perturb the homotopy relative to its boundary by [F2]. The inverse image of $\operatorname{Int}F$ is then a compact oriented one-manifold in the homotopy annulus; it is compact because the annulus image is disjoint from $L=\partial F$. Orient it using the orientations of the annulus and the normal of $F$. Its oriented boundary signs at the two ends are the intersection signs of the endpoint loops with opposite signs on the two boundary circles. The total signed boundary count is zero, so the endpoint intersection counts agree. Concatenation adds counts, hence $I_F:\pi_1(X,x_0)\to\mathbb Z$ is a homomorphism. [A1, F1, F2, given, construct]

1.2 Near a point of $K_i$, choose oriented local coordinates $(x,y,z)$ in which $K_i$ is the $x$-axis and $F$ is the half-plane $y\ge0$, $z=0$. The boundary orientation and the stated positive-meridian convention make $(x,y,z)$ ambient-positive. The small positive meridian crosses this half-plane exactly once, at $(0,\rho,0)$ for some $\rho>0$, in the $+z$ direction. Thus $\overline I_F([\mu_i])=1$ for every $i$. [F1, given, construct]

2.1 By [F3], this homomorphism factors through a homomorphism $\overline I_F:H_1(X;\mathbb Z)\to\mathbb Z$. The signed intersection convention in the Statement agrees with this induced map on the class represented by $J$. [F3, step 1.1, algebra]

3.1 By [F1], the classes $[\mu_i]$ form a basis of $H_1(X;\mathbb Z)$. The homomorphisms $\overline I_F$ and $\varphi$ agree on every basis element by step 1.2 and [F1], so they are equal. Evaluating this equality on $[J]$ gives $J\cdot F=\varphi([J])$. [F1, step 2.1, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty oriented link $L$, and a connected compact oriented spanning surface $F$ with boundary $L$.

[A1] Full AC implies dependent choice and countable choice, supplying the compact-surface normal form and Alexander-duality conventions. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]], [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]]

[F1] The compact surface has a finite cellulation, and its first homology is finitely generated and represented by integral cellular cycles. [[lem-finite-chart-surface-normal-forms-supply-jordan-disks-and-torsion-free-groups]]

[F2] Linking of disjoint oriented circles is the meridian coefficient; when a regular diagram and spanning surface are supplied it agrees with the signed intersection and mixed-crossing half-sum. [[def-one-variable-alexander-module-of-an-oriented-link]], [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]]

[F3] After moving a finite oriented link off infinity, it has a regular projection, a finite decorated immersion with finitely many mixed crossings. [[def-oriented-link-in-s-three-and-ambient-isotopy]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]], [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]

[F4] Every smooth oriented circle has a supplied connected compact oriented spanning surface, so the link-intersection theorem applies to it. [[thm-every-oriented-knot-bounds-a-seifert-surface]]

[F5] A smooth loop can be homotoped in the complement of a disjoint circle to meet a supplied spanning surface transversely. [[thm-transversality-homotopy-theorem]], [[prop-relative-transversality-preserves-a-map-on-a-closed-good-region]]



**Given:** Full AC, $L$, and $F$ as in the Statement.

1.1 Fix a finite cellulation of $F$ from [F1]. An integral cellular $1$-cycle represents each class of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$. Replace each edge with coefficient $n$ by $|n|$ parallel oriented copies, reversing orientation when $n<0$. At each vertex the cycle condition says that incoming and outgoing copies occur in equal number. Around the boundary of a small vertex disk there is therefore an adjacent incoming/outgoing pair; join that pair by a small arc and delete its endpoints, repeating finitely until all endpoints are paired. The resulting arcs can be chosen disjoint in the disk and oriented consistently with the copies. Each smoothing changes the chain only by the boundary of a $2$-chain in that disk. The result is a finite disjoint union of oriented embedded circles representing the original homology class. [A1, F1, given, construct]

1.2 For representatives $X,X'$ of the same class in $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, there is an integral singular $2$-chain $A$ in $F$ with $\partial A=X-X'$. Push the chain through a small positive normal level of $F$; its boundary is $X^+-X'^+$ and it is disjoint from any representative $Y\subset F$. Thus $X^+$ and $X'^+$ represent the same class in $H_1(S^3\setminus Y;\mathbb Z)$, so their meridian-coordinate linking sums with $Y$ agree. Varying the small positive level traces an annulus in the positive bicollar, also disjoint from $Y$, and gives the same class. [F2, given, algebra]

1.3 If $Y,Y'$ represent the same class, choose an integral $2$-chain $B$ in $F$ with $\partial B=Y-Y'$. For each circle component of $X^+$ and each circle component of $Y-Y'$, [F4] supplies a spanning surface and [F5] permits a homotopy of the other circle in its complement to make it transverse to that surface. By [F3] choose a regular diagram of the pair. By [F2], linking is the half-sum of mixed crossing signs; exchanging the two components leaves the same mixed crossings with the same signs, so linking is symmetric. Bilinearity then gives $\operatorname{lk}(X^+,Y-Y')=\operatorname{lk}(Y-Y',X^+)$. The cycle $Y-Y'$ bounds $B$ in $S^3\setminus X^+$, so its total meridian coefficient there is zero. Hence the two linking sums agree in the second variable as well. Additivity of meridian coefficients gives bilinearity in both variables. [F2, F3, F4, F5, given, algebra]

2.1 The value in the Statement is therefore independent of the chosen cycle representatives and push-off level and is bilinear on homology. In any ordered integral basis its matrix entries are $V_{ij}=\operatorname{lk}(a_i^+,a_j)$, as required. [step 1.1, step 1.2, step 1.3, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Full AC, a nonempty oriented link $L$, a connected compact oriented spanning surface $F$, an ordered basis of $H_1(F;\mathbb Z)$, and one embedded arc surgery producing $F'$.

[A1] Full AC implies dependent choice and countable choice, supplying the Alexander-duality convention and compact-surface normal form. [[def-axiom-of-choice]], [[thm-choice-implies-dependent-implies-countable-choice]], [[def-countable-choice]]

[F1] The positive-push Seifert pairing is well-defined and bilinear on the homology of every connected link surface. [[lem-link-seifert-pairing-well-defined]]

[F2] An arc surgery replaces two disks by the lateral annulus of an embedded product cylinder, leaving the oriented boundary unchanged. [[def-seifert-surface-arc-surgery]]

[F3] Mayer–Vietoris computes the homology of two surfaces glued along a common boundary circle. [[thm-mayer-vietoris-sequence-in-singular-homology]]

[F4] Linking is the signed intersection with a supplied spanning surface; linking of disjoint circles is symmetric. [[thm-linking-number-equals-signed-intersection]], [[lem-link-seifert-pairing-well-defined]], [[def-regular-oriented-link-diagram]], [[lem-every-oriented-link-admits-a-regular-projection]]



**Given:** The data of the Statement.

1.1 The two surgery disks and a narrow strip in $F$ joining them have a disk neighbourhood $D$. Replacing the disks by the lateral annulus of the cylinder changes this neighbourhood into a once-punctured torus $P$ with the same boundary $\partial D$. Write $F_0=\overline{F\setminus D}$. Any old homology class can be represented in $F_0$: replace each of its finitely many arcs through $D$ by an arc along $\partial D$, which changes the cycle by a boundary in the disk. Take open collar neighbourhoods in $F$ and $F'$ so that $F_0$ and respectively $D$ or $P$ form open covers whose intersection retracts onto $\partial D$. In the Mayer–Vietoris sequence [F3], the map from $H_0(\partial D;\mathbb Z)=\mathbb Z$ to the direct sum of the two $H_0$ groups is $n\mapsto(n,-n)$ and is injective. For $F=F_0\cup D$, the $H_1$ map from the intersection circle has image generated by $([\partial D],0)$, since $H_1(D;\mathbb Z)=0$. For $F'=F_0\cup P$, the same image is generated by $([\partial D],0)$ because the oriented boundary of $P$ is zero in $H_1(P;\mathbb Z)$, while $H_1(P;\mathbb Z)\cong\mathbb Z^2$ on its longitudinal and meridional curves. Thus $H_1(F')\cong H_1(F)\oplus\mathbb Z^2$, with the old classes as a direct summand. Choose the added basis classes $b,c$ from those two curves; together with the old basis they are an integral basis. [A1, F2, F3, given, construct]

2.1 The surgery retains the old oriented surface outside the two attaching disks, so its positive normal there is unchanged and the old matrix block remains $V$. Use product coordinates $(t,w)$ on the cylinder, with $w\in D^2$, and take $c=\{t_0\}\times\partial D^2$. Let $b$ follow one longitudinal side of the tube and return through $F_0$; it crosses each cross-section disk once. The disks $\{t_0\}\times D^2$ and their sufficiently close parallel disks miss every old basis curve and its push-off, so [F4] gives zero for the two Seifert pairings between $c$ and every old basis curve. Along the lateral annulus, the positive normal points either out of or into the solid cylinder. If it points out, the radius-one cross-section disk misses $b^+$, giving $V(b,c)=0$, while the disk of slightly larger radius bounds $c^+$ and meets $b$ once; it gives $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=+1$ after orienting $c$, hence $V(c,b)=+1$ by the symmetry in [F4]. If it points in, the radius-one disk meets $b^+$ once, giving $V(b,c)=+1$ after orienting $c$, while the disk of slightly smaller radius bounds $c^+$ and misses $b$, giving $\operatorname{lk}(b,c^+)=0$ and therefore $V(c,b)=0$. These intersection statements follow from the explicit single transverse point in the product coordinates and [F4]. In either case the concentric parallel meridians have $V(c,c)=0$. The remaining entries involving $b$ are integers $x$, $y$, and $z=\operatorname{lk}(b^+,b)$. Thus in the ordered basis $(a_1,\ldots,a_m,b,c)$ the matrix has exactly one of the two displayed forms. [F1, F2, F4, step 1.1, construct, algebra] ∎

**Given:** Full AC, an oriented knot, its Seifert matrix $V$, and an Alexander root $\omega_0\ne1$.

[A1] Full AC and the chosen surface/basis supply a finite real Seifert matrix. [[def-knot-seifert-pairing-and-matrix]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]

[F1] $H_{e^{i\theta}}$ is a continuous Hermitian matrix family, and its singular parameters away from $1$ are exactly the zeros of a nonzero Alexander polynomial. [[def-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-and-signature]], [[lem-levine-tristram-hermitian-form-singular-set]], [[lem-square-seifert-presentation-and-alexander-normalization]]

[F2] Ordered Hermitian eigenvalues vary continuously, indeed Lipschitzly in operator norm. [[lem-complex-hermitian-eigenvalues-lipschitz]]

[F3] A continuous real function on an interval cannot take both positive and negative values without vanishing between them. [[thm-intermediate-value]]



1.1 The entries of $H_{e^{i\theta}}$ are continuous functions of $\theta$. By [F2], each ordered eigenvalue $\lambda_j(\theta)$ is continuous. The determinant presentation in [F1] is a nonzero Laurent polynomial because its value at $t=1$ is $\pm1$; hence it has only finitely many roots on the unit circle. Choose $\epsilon>0$ so that each punctured one-sided arc $(\theta_0-\epsilon,\theta_0)$ and $(\theta_0,\theta_0+\epsilon)$ contains no other root. On each such arc, [F1] makes every eigenvalue nonzero. [A1, F1, F2, given, choose]

2.1 On either arc, a continuous real function $\lambda_j$ that never vanishes has constant sign: if it took both signs, [F3] would give a zero. Thus every positive/negative eigenvalue count is constant on each one-sided arc, and the signature there is a fixed integer. Each one-sided limit is that integer. [F1, F3, step 1.1, algebra] ∎
